case_studies.title: PyroDash: Cost-Efficient Token-Level Small-Large Language Model Collaborative Inference
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide strong reasoning capabilities but are expensive to serve at scale, whereas small language models (SLMs) are cheaper but less reliable on difficult problems. We introduce PyroDash, a cost-aware framework for token-level SLM-LLM collaborative inference. During generation, the SLM decides whether to request assistance by emitting a control token. A Collaborate Engine then sends the query and partial reasoning trace to a frozen LLM for completion through a single handoff. The policy is internalized in the SLM, requiring neither a separate router, LLM retraining
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of expensive large language models by creating PyroDash, a framework that collaborates between small and large language models for cost-efficient inference, resulting in stronger reasoning capabilities at a lower cost. The researchers built a cost-aware framework that enables small language models to request assistance from large language models when needed. This framework achieves reliable results without requiring retraining of the large language model.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for language model deployments, here is what to consider: assess your current language model setup to see if PyroDash can help reduce costs, evaluate the feasibility of integrating PyroDash into your existing architecture, and consider the potential benefits of collaborative inference for your specific use case. This flags a risk: if your organization uses large language models at scale, check your current costs and explore alternatives like PyroDash to optimize expenses. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of language model deployments.
case_studies.relevance_tag: MLOps, AI deployment, SaaS tooling, cloud infrastructure
case_studies.score_reasoning: PyroDash introduces a novel approach to cost-aware, collaborative inference for large and small language models, with direct implications for AI deployment and infrastructure.

case_studies.abstract: Fine-tuning has been widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) for domain-specific tasks. Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. PortLLM is a training-free and data-free scheme used to adapt LLMs after continual pretraining. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of adapting large language models to new tasks by explaining why some methods work well over time. The researchers built on existing methods like low-rank adaptation to improve the performance of these models. The result is a better understanding of how to fine-tune language models without needing a lot of data or computational power.

case_studies.title: Sound Probabilistic Safety Bounds for Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: We propose a novel framework for computing rigorous bounds on the probability that a large language model (LLM) generates harmful output to a given prompt. We study a new application of the Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals to obtain probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds for this problem. case_studies.title: PoTRE: Test-Time Reasoning inspired by Cognitive Heterogeneity
case_studies.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at many tasks, they frequently struggle with complex reasoning that requires long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models struggling with complex reasoning tasks by introducing a new framework called PoTRE, which uses four different agents to improve inference, resulting in better performance on tasks that require long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. The researchers built a heterogeneous framework that decouples inference into four agents, leading to more robust and flexible reasoning. This framework can potentially improve the accuracy of language models used in various applications.

case_studies.title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values
case_studies.abstract: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to be culturally biased toward Western norms. This results in the mishandling of local values in multilingual societies such as Sri Lanka that have their unique cultural dynamics. Existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lankan-contextualized values in its official language Sinhala, hindering culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of culturally biased large language models by creating LKValues, a survey-grounded resource suite for Sri Lankan value alignment. The result is a more culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning of language models for the Sri Lankan context. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work in the UK.

case_studies.title: On the Systematic Challenges of Culturally Loaded Machine Translation: Dream of the Red Chamber as the Cultural Lens
case_studies.abstract: Culturally loaded translation poses unique challenges for machine translation (MT), as meanings are deeply embedded in socio-cultural contexts beyond surface linguistic forms. Although large language models (LLMs) have enabled MT systems to achieve human-like quality in many scenarios, their ability to handle culturally loaded expressions remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically investigate the challenges posed by culturally loaded translation in LLM-based MT systems. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of culturally loaded machine translation by investigating the challenges it poses to large language models. The authors built a bilingual dataset from a culturally representative corpus to test these challenges. The result is a deeper understanding of the limitations of current machine translation systems in handling culturally loaded expressions.

case_studies.title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate in executable environments where a failed attempt produces actionable feedback rather than merely an incorrect answer. Existing cost-aware systems typically treat such failures as cascade decisions: try a cheap model first, then escalate hard cases to a stronger and more expensive model. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of deciding when to escalate to a more expensive model after a coding agent fails, by building a system called CodeRescue that determines the best recovery routing based on budget and execution feedback. The result is a more efficient use of resources in coding agent deployment. This research is relevant to IT work in terms of optimizing resource allocation in cloud infrastructure.
